blocks.text: This closing topic is not new material, it is the hard won wisdom that ties together everything covered across this whole course, the practices that separate someone who knows the individual techniques from someone who applies them well in real projects.
1. Never Modify Raw Data In Place

Always work on a copy and keep the original file or table untouched. If a cleaning step turns out to be wrong, or a business rule changes later, you need to be able to go back to the true original and redo the cleaning. Overwriting the source is a one way door that is very expensive to walk back through.

code.content:
raw_df = pd.read_csv('original_data.csv')   # never touched again
work_df = raw_df.copy()                       # all cleaning happens on this copy

blocks.text: 2. Document Every Decision, Not Just the Action

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: A comment or log entry like "dropped 12 rows with age over 120, treated as data entry errors based on team discussion" is far more valuable six months later than silently dropping the rows with no record. Someone will eventually ask why the row count changed.

blocks.text: 3. Keep a Before and After Comparison
Record row counts and key summary statistics before and after each major transformation, so an unexpected change is caught immediately rather than silently propagating downstream.

code.content:
before_rows = len(df)
before_mean_age = df['age'].mean()

df = clean(df)

print(f"rows: {before_rows} -> {len(df)}")
print(f"mean age: {before_mean_age:.1f} -> {df['age'].mean():.1f}")

blocks.text: This connects back to the Data Quality Assessment topic early in this course. Understanding the shape and problems of the data first prevents wasted effort cleaning things that were never actually broken, or missing things that were.
5. Prefer Reusable, Tested Functions Over One Off Code

This connects to the Automated Data Cleaning and Cleaning Pipelines topics. Code that will only ever run once on one dataset is fine for quick exploration, but any cleaning logic that will run again on new data deserves to be a real, tested function.
6. Be Skeptical of Your Own Cleaning Code
Test it on deliberately edge case inputs: an empty dataframe, a single row, or a value at the exact boundary of a range check. Edge cases are where cleaning bugs hide.
7. Involve Domain Experts for Genuine Judgment Calls

A data scientist alone often cannot correctly decide whether an unusual value is a real anomaly worth keeping or an error worth removing. Someone who understands the actual business or domain the data represents should be consulted for the genuinely ambiguous cases.

blocks.text: 9. Common Mistakes Even After Learning the Techniques

items: Rushing straight to cleaning without first assessing data quality.
Cleaning so aggressively that legitimate signal is thrown away along with genuine noise.
Never revisiting cleaning logic as a dataset or business evolves over time.

blocks.text: Every model, every dashboard, every business decision downstream is only as trustworthy as the data cleaning that came before it. It rarely gets the credit, but it is the foundation everything else stands on.
